title: The Cat Boat
altText: A black-and-white etching of a small sailboat on the water, made with fine lines and shading. The title names the boat as a cat boat; further details have not been confirmed from the record.

source.verifiedBy: Art Institute of Chicago API record: title, artist (Edward Hopper, American, 1882-1967), date, medium, place of origin, credit line and public-domain flag (false) read from the record. The record has no description or subject terms. No image linked because the work is in copyright.

context: Made in 1922 by the American artist Edward Hopper. The museum record lists an etching on off-white wove paper and the title The Cat Boat, and gives no description. A catboat is a type of small sailboat with a single sail. Hopper made a number of etchings in the early 1920s before becoming better known as a painter.

descriptions.k: This is a picture of a little sailboat, made with lines. It is black and white. Can you imagine the wind and the water? Where do you think the boat is going?
descriptions.g12: Edward Hopper made this picture of a small boat, called a cat boat. It is an etching, which means he scratched lines into metal and printed them. There is no color, just black lines on cream paper. How do the lines show water, wind, or sunlight?
descriptions.g35: Edward Hopper is famous for paintings, but he also made etchings. The Cat Boat (1922) is a print made by cutting lines into a metal plate, inking it, and pressing it on paper. A catboat is a small sailboat with one sail. How can black lines show water and light? What would you add in color?
descriptions.g68: Hopper made The Cat Boat in 1922 as an etching, scratching lines into a metal plate to print on paper. The title names a type of small sailboat, but the museum gives no further description. How can only line and tone show water, air, and sunlight, and how might Hopper's later paintings of quiet places connect to this print?
descriptions.g910: The Cat Boat (1922) is one of Hopper's early etchings, made before his reputation as a painter was established. The museum offers no description beyond title and medium, so the print must speak through line, tone, and composition. Consider how etching's incised lines create light and shadow, and how a simple subject like a small sailboat can carry mood without narrative.
descriptions.g1112: Hopper's etching The Cat Boat (1922) represents a period when printmaking offered him both income and a laboratory for compositional ideas that later informed his paintings. The museum record supplies only title, date, and medium, so interpretation depends on visual evidence. How do line density and tone construct light, water, and stillness, and what can an early print suggest about continuities in Hopper's sensibility without overreading?

safety.method: Title, artist and medium (etching) checked against the Art Institute of Chicago record; no concerning terms. The record has no description, so student text relies on the title and medium; a person must confirm the image before release. The image itself was not visually inspected.

teacherNote.context: A 1922 etching by Edward Hopper in the Art Institute of Chicago. The museum record gives only the title and medium, so a person must review the image. The work is in copyright, so no image is linked yet.
directions: Have students scratch a simple boat scene into a foam plate and print it in one color.
Ask students to compare how dark and light are shown in a pencil drawing and a print.
Discuss how an artist can express mood without color.
